title: Myrmidons and Dolopians
greek: quis talia fando Myrmidonum Dolopumve aut duri miles Ulixi temperet a lacrimis?
short: The Myrmidons were Achilles' men from Phthia, the Dolopians a Thessalian people under his father Peleus; together they stand for the followers of Achilles and his son Pyrrhus.
body: Aeneas opens his story by saying that not even the hardest enemy, a Myrmidon, a Dolopian or a soldier of 'stern Ulysses' (Ulixes, the Latin name for Odysseus), could hold back tears at such a tale. The Myrmidons were Achilles' contingent in the Iliad; the Dolopians were a Thessalian tribe whom Peleus gave to Phoenix to rule (Il. 9.484). After Achilles' death they followed his son Neoptolemus (Pyrrhus), who leads the sack of Priam's palace later in this book. The opening, 'Dreadful, O Queen, is the woe thou bidst me recall' (infandum, regina, iubes renovare dolorem, 2.3), echoes Odysseus' reluctance to tell his sorrows to the Phaeacians (Od. 9.12-13), and makes Book 2 the Aeneid's counterpart to Odysseus' tales in Odyssey 9-12.

title: The Wooden Horse
greek: instar montis equum divina Palladis arte aedificant
short: The Greeks build a horse 'as big as a mountain' with Minerva's help, pretend it is a votive offering for their return, and hide soldiers in its belly.
body: The Wooden Horse is mentioned in the Odyssey (4.271-89, 8.492-520, 11.523-32), where Demodocus sings of it and Odysseus is its leader, and it was told at length in the lost cyclic epics Little Iliad and Sack of Troy (Iliou Persis). Virgil fills the story with the language of pregnancy and birth: its 'womb' (uterus, alvus) is filled with armed men, it is 'big with arms' (feta armis, 2.238), and at night it 'restores them to the air'. The wood is variously fir (2.16), maple (2.112) and oak (2.186) and pine (2.258), an inconsistency commentators have noticed. The Greeks pretend it is a votive offering (votum) for their safe return, a gift to Minerva, so to destroy it would be sacrilege; Sinon's story turns on this. Conington notes the Homeric and cyclic sources.

title: Laocoon
greek: Laocoon ardens summa decurrit ab arce
short: Laocoon, priest of Neptune, warns the Trojans against the horse and strikes it with his spear; the hollow groan should have revealed the trick.
body: Laocoon was a Trojan priest; his story was told in the cyclic Sack of Troy and in a lost tragedy by Sophocles. In Virgil he is the voice of good sense, and his speech is full of contempt for Greek craft: 'is it thus we know Ulysses?' The spear he throws makes the hollow womb of the horse 'groan', and Aeneas comments that if the gods' will and the people's minds had not been 'infatuate' (laeva), Troy would still stand (2.54-6). Page notes the poignant apostrophe to Priam's towers. Laocoon's death by the serpents (2.199-227) is then read by the Trojans as punishment for sacrilege, which gives the horse its entry. His warning words follow in the next note.

title: 'I fear the Greeks even bearing gifts'
greek: quidquid id est, timeo Danaos et dona ferentes
short: Laocoon's warning became a proverb: beware of gifts from an enemy. The 'gift' theme (donum) runs through the whole story of the horse.
body: Danai is one of Virgil's names for the Greeks (from Danaus, a legendary king of Argos), alongside Argivi, Achivi and Pelasgi. The line, timeo Danaos et dona ferentes, has passed into proverbial use in English as 'beware of Greeks bearing gifts'. The horse is repeatedly called a gift: 'the deadly gift of Minerva the Virgin' (donum exitiale Minervae, 2.31), a 'gift of Greece'. In the ancient world gifts created obligation and could carry concealed harm; Greek proverbs about 'gifts of enemies' that are 'no gifts' go back to Sophocles (Ajax 665). Et here means 'even': Laocoon fears the Greeks even when they come with offerings to the gods.

anchor: if Fortune hath made Sinon unhappy
title: Sinon and his lying tale
greek: nec, si miserum Fortuna Sinonem finxit, vanum etiam mendacemque improba finget
short: Sinon, a Greek left behind on purpose, wins the Trojans' pity with a brilliantly crafted false story; Aeneas calls him a single crime from which to learn all Greek treachery.
body: Sinon's speech is a masterpiece of persuasive lying. He begins by swearing to tell the truth and plays on the Trojans' feelings: pity (he is an outcast), curiosity (he breaks off his story, 2.101-4), and hatred of Ulysses, whom he blames for his ruin. He uses true facts (Palamedes' death, Iphigenia's sacrifice, the theft of the Palladium) to make false ones believable. Aeneas' comment 'from a single crime learn all' (crimine ab uno disce omnis, 2.65-6) generalises his treachery to all Greeks. The narrator's bitterness frames everything: 'So by Sinon's wiles and craft and perjury the thing gained belief' (2.195-8), we 'whom neither Diomedes nor Achilles of Larissa, nor ten years nor a thousand ships' could conquer. Ancient readers admired the speech as rhetoric, and it was studied in the schools.

title: The sacrifice of Iphigenia
greek: sanguine placastis ventos et virgine caesa
short: Sinon's oracle alludes to the sacrifice of Agamemnon's daughter Iphigenia at Aulis, which calmed the winds so that the Greek fleet could sail to Troy.
body: The oracle Sinon reports ('With blood and a slain maiden you appeased the winds') refers to Iphigenia, sacrificed by her father Agamemnon at Aulis to Artemis, who was holding back the fleet with contrary winds. The story was told in the Cypria and is central in Aeschylus' Agamemnon (184-247), Euripides' Iphigenia at Aulis and Lucretius' famous attack on religion (1.84-101, tantum religio potuit suadere malorum). Virgil does not name her: the allusion is enough for an educated reader, and the gods' demand for a human life now falls, Sinon says, on him. The pattern of one life for many returns at 5.815 (unum pro multis dabitur caput) with Palinurus.

anchor: the salted corn, and the chaplets
title: Sacrificial rites: salted meal and fillets
greek: mihi sacra parari et salsae fruges et circum tempora vittae
short: Sinon describes the preparations for his sacrifice as for a Roman animal victim: salted meal sprinkled on the head and woollen fillets (vittae) bound round the temples.
body: In Roman sacrifice the victim's head was sprinkled with mola salsa, coarse meal mixed with salt (hence 'immolate', from mola), and decorated with vittae, woollen ribbons or fillets. Virgil gives a Greek scene Roman ritual colour. The vittae recur through the book: Sinon swears by the 'fillets of the gods' he wore as a victim (2.156), Laocoon's fillets are spattered with venom (2.221), and Panthus' 'Apollo's fillet' (2.430) fails to protect him. Page explains the details. The ritual vocabulary makes Sinon's lies sound authentic and frames the fall of Troy as a sequence of sacrifices, true and false, ending in the death of Priam at an altar.

title: The Palladium
greek: fatale ... Palladium
short: The Palladium was an ancient image of Pallas on which Troy's safety depended; Diomedes and Ulysses stole it, and Sinon claims the horse was built to atone for the theft.
body: The Palladium was a small wooden statue of Pallas (Athena/Minerva), said to have fallen from heaven, which guaranteed Troy's safety while it remained in the city; hence 'fated' (fatale). The theft by Diomedes and Ulysses was told in the Little Iliad. Sinon describes portents in the Greek camp: flames from the statue's eyes, salt sweat, and the image leaping three times with shield and spear. 'The Tritonian' is Minerva, so called from lake Triton in Libya, near which she was said to be born, or from a river Triton in Boeotia; the title (Tritonia) recurs at 2.171, 226 and 615. Romans believed the Palladium was actually brought to Italy and kept in the temple of Vesta, which makes Sinon's story more pointed for Virgil's readers.

title: The death of Laocoon
greek: gemini a Tenedo tranquilla per alta ... angues
short: Two serpents from the sea kill Laocoon and his sons at the altar, then take refuge under Minerva's shield: the Trojans read this as punishment and admit the horse.
body: This is one of the most celebrated scenes in the poem. The serpents come over a calm sea from Tenedos, the Greek base; their blood-red crests and hissing tongues are described with vivid sound-play. They kill Laocoon's two sons and then Laocoon himself, who cries out 'as when, bellowing, a bull shakes the wavering axe from his neck' (2.223-4): the priest who was sacrificing a bull becomes himself a sacrificial victim. The serpents then hide at the feet of Minerva's statue in her citadel temple, revealing which god sent them. The scene is closely related to the marble group of Laocoon and his sons (Vatican Museums), rediscovered in Rome in 1506; whether the sculpture or the poem came first is debated. G. E. Lessing's essay Laokoon (1766) used the comparison to distinguish poetry and visual art.

anchor: four times in the very gateway
title: Omens ignored: the horse halts four times
greek: quater ipso in limine portae substitit, atque utero sonitum quater arma dedere
short: Stumbling at a threshold was a bad omen to Romans; the horse halts four times in the gate and the arms clash inside, but the 'infatuate' Trojans press on.
body: To stumble at the threshold was a notorious ill omen in Roman belief (compare the custom of carrying a bride over it). The repeated clashing of arms inside the horse is a second warning. The Trojans pull down part of their own walls, a further symbolic violation, and drag the horse in with boys and unmarried girls singing hymns and touching the rope as in a religious procession. Aeneas' cry 'O native land! O Ilium, house of gods' is an apostrophe that recalls Ennius' tragic style (Andromache's lament, O pater, o patria, o Priami domus). Then Cassandra prophesies in vain. The Trojans, 'to whom that day was our last', deck the shrines with festal boughs: dramatic irony is total.

anchor: Even then Cassandra opens her lips
title: Cassandra
greek: tunc etiam fatis aperit Cassandra futuris ora dei iussu non umquam credita Teucris
short: Cassandra, Priam's daughter, was given prophecy by Apollo and then cursed so that no one would believe her; she foresees the fall of Troy in vain.
body: In the usual story Apollo gave Cassandra the gift of prophecy to win her love, and when she refused him he made her prophecies never believed (Aeschylus, Agamemnon 1202-12). Virgil compresses this into 'lips at a god's bidding never believed'. She reappears in this book: Coroebus, who came to Troy for love of her, dies trying to rescue her as she is dragged from Minerva's temple (2.341-6, 403-8), the crime of Ajax son of Oileus. In Book 3 Anchises remembers that Cassandra alone foretold Hesperia (3.182-7). Her fate after the sack, as Agamemnon's captive killed with him at Mycenae, is not told by Virgil.

title: Hector's ghost
greek: in somnis, ecce, ante oculos maestissimus Hector visus adesse mihi
short: Hector appears to Aeneas in a dream, mangled as when Achilles dragged him, and hands over to him the gods of Troy and the mission to found a new city.
body: Dream-figures who visit a sleeper are Homeric (Patroclus' ghost appears to Achilles, Il. 23.65-107). Hector appears as he was after Achilles dragged him behind his chariot (Il. 22.395-404), black with dust and blood, with swollen, pierced feet. Aeneas, half-forgetting he is dead, greets him as 'O light of Dardania', and contrasts him with the Hector who returned in Achilles' armour (taken from Patroclus, Il. 17) and set fire to the Greek ships (Il. 15-16). Hector tells him to flee: 'If Troy towers might be defended by strength of hand, this hand too had been their defence.' He entrusts to Aeneas Troy's 'holy things and household gods' and brings out Vesta and the everlasting fire. The passing of Troy's mission from its greatest warrior to Aeneas is the turning point of the book.

title: Vesta and the everlasting fire
greek: sic ait, et manibus vittas Vestamque potentem aeternumque adytis effert penetralibus ignem
short: Vesta was the goddess of the hearth; her undying fire, tended at Rome by the Vestal Virgins, was believed to have come from Troy with Aeneas.
body: Vesta (Greek Hestia) was the goddess of the hearth, of household and state. In Rome her round temple in the Forum held the eternal flame and, according to tradition, sacred objects brought from Troy, including the Palladium; the flame was kept alight by the Vestal Virgins, and its going out was a dreadful omen. By having Hector bring out 'Vesta' (her image or her fire) and the 'eternal fire' from the inner shrine, Virgil traces Rome's most sacred cult directly to Troy and to Aeneas' rescue. Vesta returns in Jupiter's prophecy as 'hoar Vesta' (cana Vesta, 1.292), and Augustus, who became pontifex maximus in 12 BC, set up a shrine of Vesta in his own house on the Palatine.

title: Ucalegon: the neighbour's house on fire
greek: iam proximus ardet Ucalegon
short: Ucalegon, one of Priam's old counsellors in the Iliad, stands here for his house: 'already neighbour Ucalegon is ablaze', a phrase that became proverbial.
body: Ucalegon appears in Iliad 3.148 among the elders who sit with Priam on the walls of Troy. Virgil uses his name for his house, a figure of speech (metonymy) like 'Apollo' for Apollo's temple at 3.275, as Page and Conington both note. The effect is vivid and personal: the fire is next door. Juvenal later echoes the phrase (Satires 3.198-9), and 'iam proximus ardet Ucalegon' became a proverb for danger at one's own doorstep. Deiphobus, whose house falls first, was Priam's son who married Helen after Paris' death; Aeneas meets his mutilated ghost at 6.494-534. The 'Sigean bay' is the strait near Cape Sigeum at the mouth of the Hellespont.

title: Panthus: 'We have been Trojans'
greek: venit summa dies et ineluctabile tempus Dardaniae. fuimus Troes, fuit Ilium
short: Panthus, priest of Apollo, announces Troy's end in the perfect tense: 'we have been Trojans, Ilium has been', that is, they are no more.
body: Panthus, son of Othrys, priest of Apollo on the citadel, runs out carrying the sacred objects and his grandson: a figure of pietas like Aeneas himself. His words use the Latin perfect tense with the force 'we were (and are no longer)': fuimus Troes, fuit Ilium et ingens gloria Teucrorum. Mackail renders the sense ('No more are we a Trojan people; Ilium ... is no more'). Page draws attention to the repetition of the verb. Panthus also says 'Angry Jupiter hath cast all into the scale of Argos', a reminder that the gods have abandoned Troy. In the Iliad Panthous is an elder and father of Polydamas and Euphorbus. He dies at 2.429-30, unprotected by his piety or Apollo's fillet.

title: 'The one safety for the conquered is to hope for none'
greek: una salus victis nullam sperare salutem
short: Aeneas rouses his small band to a hopeless last stand with a paradox that became a famous maxim of desperate courage.
body: Aeneas' speech to his volunteers is a speech of despair turned to courage: the gods have left their shrines (a Roman belief that gods abandoned a city before its fall, compare the ritual evocatio, the calling out of an enemy's gods before a siege), so the only course is to 'die, and rush on their weapons'. The final line plays on salus, 'safety' or 'salvation', used twice. The scene characterises Aeneas as a warrior of furor at this point in his story: 'Fury and wrath drive me headlong' (2.316). Readers often contrast this young, impetuous Aeneas with the duty-bound leader of later books, and his narrative to Dido is in part a story of learning that his duty lies elsewhere.

title: The wolf simile
greek: inde, lupi ceu raptores atra in nebula
short: Aeneas' band moves through the city like ravenous wolves in fog, driven by hunger, with cubs waiting at home: an image of desperate, blind aggression.
body: Homer often compares warriors to wolves (Il. 16.156-63, the Myrmidons). Virgil's version stresses blindness ('black fog') and hunger, and adds the cubs waiting 'with throats unslaked', which recalls the families the Trojans are leaving. It is unusual for the narrator to compare himself and his comrades to predators; some readers see a darker side of heroic fury. Night's 'sheltering shadow' and the inexpressible horror ('Who may unfold in speech that night's horror ...?', 2.361-2) follow, in the manner of Homer's inability topos ('not if I had ten tongues', Il. 2.489).

title: Coroebus and the stolen armour: dolus an virtus
greek: dolus an virtus, quis in hoste requirat?
short: Coroebus urges the Trojans to put on Greek armour: 'trickery or valour, who asks which against an enemy?' The ruse works at first, then kills them.
body: Coroebus, son of Mygdon, a Phrygian ally, had come to Troy for love of Cassandra (2.341-6). After killing Androgeos' band, he proposes the disguise, and the Trojans take on the 'Greek' qualities of trickery that they have just suffered. His maxim, dolus an virtus, quis in hoste requirat, raises the ethical question of whether deceit is legitimate in war, a question the whole book has posed through Sinon and the horse. The trick turns against them: they are stoned by their own side from the temple roof because of their Greek crests (2.410-12), and the Greeks recognise the 'lying weapons' and the 'alien tone' of their speech.

anchor: was being dragged with disordered tresses
title: Cassandra dragged from Minerva's temple
greek: ecce trahebatur passis Priameia virgo crinibus a templo Cassandra adytisque Minervae
short: Ajax son of Oileus tears Cassandra from Minerva's shrine; the sacrilege kills Coroebus and his comrades and later wrecks the Greek fleet.
body: This is the crime Juno mentioned at 1.39-45. Cassandra lifts her 'blazing eyes' to heaven, 'her eyes, for fetters locked her delicate hands', a famous effect of repetition. Coroebus charges to rescue her and the Trojans are caught between Greek counter-attack and the missiles of their own countrymen. The Greeks are compared to winds clashing in a storm, with Nereus, the old sea-god, stirring the sea with his trident (2.416-19), a storm simile that recalls Book 1. 'The goddess armipotent' (armipotens, 'mighty in arms') at whose altar Coroebus falls is Minerva herself.

anchor: gods' ways are not as ours
title: Rhipeus: dis aliter visum
greek: cadit et Ripheus, iustissimus unus qui fuit in Teucris et servantissimus aequi (dis aliter visum)
short: The most just of the Trojans dies, and Aeneas comments only 'the gods saw it otherwise': a short phrase of resignation before divine inscrutability.
body: Dis aliter visum, literally 'to the gods it seemed otherwise', is Page's 'Heaven willed it otherwise', an interjectional phrase of 'pious but melancholy acquiescence in what is inscrutable'. Rhipeus' death raises the problem of divine justice already posed in the proem (1.11): goodness gives no protection, as Panthus' death in the next line also shows ('nor did all thy goodness, O Panthus, nor Apollo's fillet protect thy fall'). Page compares Odyssey 1.234. Dante later placed Rhipeus, surprisingly, among the just souls in his Paradise (Paradiso 20.67-72), as an example of God's justice being beyond human understanding, an ironic answer to Virgil's line.

title: Pyrrhus (Neoptolemus) like a snake
greek: vestibulum ante ipsum primoque in limine Pyrrhus exsultat telis et luce coruscus aena: qualis ubi in lucem coluber
short: Achilles' son Pyrrhus, also called Neoptolemus, bursts into Priam's palace gleaming like a snake that has sloughed its skin, an image of renewed, deadly youth.
body: Pyrrhus ('Red-haired', from Greek pyrrhos) is the other name of Neoptolemus ('New War'), son of Achilles, brought to Troy after his father's death because the city could not fall without him. The simile adapts Iliad 22.93-5, where Hector waiting for Achilles is like a snake fed on poisonous herbs; Virgil adds the shedding of the old skin (exuviae), and the play is pointed, since Pyrrhus is a 'renewed' Achilles in shining bronze. Mackail's 'fresh from his weeds outworn' renders positis novus exuviis. With him come Automedon, Achilles' charioteer, and the 'Scyrian' men from Scyros, where Pyrrhus grew up. He smashes the doors, opening to view 'the secret chambers of Priam and the kings of old'. Virgil's Georgics (3.437-9) uses the same lines of a snake.

title: The death of Priam at the altar
greek: Priamumque per aras sanguine foedantem quos ipse sacraverat ignes
short: Priam, after seeing his son Polites killed, curses Pyrrhus, is dragged through his son's blood and butchered at his own household altar: the climax of the sack.
body: Priam takes refuge with Hecuba and her daughters at the altar in the palace court, under an ancient laurel (the altar of Zeus Herkeios, protector of the enclosure). Pyrrhus kills Polites before his parents' eyes, and Priam reproaches him: Achilles, whose son he claims to be, respected a suppliant's rights and returned Hector's body (Iliad 24). Pyrrhus' answer, 'tell my father of my degenerate deeds ... Now die', is chillingly laconic. The killing at the altar is the ultimate sacrilege, since suppliants at an altar were under divine protection. Hecuba's 'hundred daughters' (centum nurus, really daughters-in-law) and Priam's 'fifty bridal chambers' come from Iliad 6.242-50. The death of Priam at the altar was told in the cyclic Sack of Troy.

anchor: revered a suppliant's right and trust
title: Supplication and Achilles' example
greek: sed iura fidemque supplicis erubuit corpusque exsangue sepulcro reddidit Hectoreum
short: Priam reminds Pyrrhus that Achilles 'blushed' before a suppliant's rights and returned Hector's body: supplication was a sacred claim on mercy.
body: Supplication (Latin supplex, Greek hiketeia) was a ritual act: the suppliant clasped the knees or touched the chin of the person begged, or took refuge at an altar, and was protected by Zeus/Jupiter. In Iliad 24 Priam supplicates Achilles in his hut, kissing the hands that killed his sons, and Achilles, moved by pity, releases Hector's body. Virgil's verb erubuit, 'he blushed at', 'he respected', captures the shame (Greek aidos) that restrains violence against suppliants. Priam's speech shows that Pyrrhus is a degenerate son of a hero, and it frames the problem of mercy that returns at the very end of the poem, where Turnus supplicates Aeneas (12.930-8). Achemenides in Book 3 is another suppliant (3.607).

title: 'A body without a name': Priam and Pompey
greek: iacet ingens litore truncus, avulsumque umeris caput et sine nomine corpus
short: Priam's headless trunk lying on the shore recalls the death of Pompey the Great, beheaded on the Egyptian shore in 48 BC, as Servius already noted.
body: Oddly, Priam was killed in his palace, yet his body lies 'along the shore'. Servius explains the detail as an allusion to Pompey the Great, murdered and beheaded on the beach at Pelusium in Egypt in 48 BC, whose body was left unburied; Servius also notes that Pompey had ruled over Asia, as Priam had been 'lord over so many peoples and lands of Asia'. Page agrees that Virgil must have had Pompey's fate in mind. Servius also connects the passage with a tragedy by Pacuvius. 'Without a name' means without identity or tomb: the great king becomes anonymous, the extreme of the fall from greatness. The allusion brings the civil wars of Virgil's own lifetime into the fall of Troy.

title: The Helen episode (2.567-88): genuine or not?
greek: iamque adeo super unus eram, cum limina Vestae servantem et tacitam secreta in sede latentem Tyndarida aspicio
short: Aeneas' near-killing of Helen, 'the daughter of Tyndarus', is absent from the main manuscripts and preserved only by Servius; whether Virgil wrote it is debated.
body: Mackail prints the 22 lines in square brackets because they do not appear in the major ancient manuscripts. They survive only in the expanded Servius commentary (the note on 2.566), which says they were cut by Varius and Tucca, Virgil's literary executors; Conington prints the passage. Against authenticity: in 6.511-27 Deiphobus tells a different story, with Helen betraying him to the Greeks in his house, and the language has been thought un-Virgilian; for it: Venus' speech (2.594-620), with its 'Not the hated face of the Laconian woman' (2.601), seems to answer something, and without the lines there is an abrupt transition. Page states the arguments on both sides. R. G. Austin (Classical Quarterly 1961, and his 1964 commentary) defended them as Virgil's; G. P. Goold (Harvard Studies in Classical Philology 74, 1970) is among the leading modern critics who reject them. Tyndarus was Helen's mortal father (her divine father was Jupiter).

anchor: the gods, the gods in anger
title: Venus reveals the gods destroying Troy
greek: divum inclementia, divum, has evertit opes
short: Venus removes the mist from Aeneas' eyes so he can see Neptune, Juno, Minerva and Jupiter himself tearing Troy down: not Helen or Paris but the gods are to blame.
body: Venus' rebuke turns Aeneas from revenge to his duty to his family. Then she grants him a vision normally hidden from mortals, modelled on Athena removing the mist from Diomedes' eyes (Il. 5.127-8). Neptune, who with Apollo built Troy's walls, now shakes them with his trident; Juno holds the Scaean gate, the main gate of Troy in the Iliad; Minerva ('Tritonian Pallas') sits on the citadel with her storm-cloud and Gorgon (the aegis, bearing the Gorgon's head); and Jupiter himself encourages the Greeks. The repetition 'the gods, the gods' (divum ... divum) insists on divine responsibility. Conington and Page discuss whether nimbus means a bright halo or a dark storm cloud. 'Awful faces ... divine majesties' is another unfinished half-line (2.623).

title: Troy falls like an ancient ash tree
greek: ac veluti summis antiquam in montibus ornum ...
short: Troy collapses like a mountain ash hacked by woodcutters, which totters, groans and falls: the city is a living thing dying under repeated blows.
body: The simile develops Homeric tree similes for falling warriors (Il. 4.482-7, 13.389-91, 16.482-6), but Virgil applies it to a whole city. The tree is old (antiquam), hacked by competing farmers (agricolae), and personified: it 'nods' with its trembling 'tresses' (comae, foliage and hair), 'groans' and 'tears itself away'. The city's age, its long history and the effort needed to bring it down all appear in the image. 'Neptunian Troy' recalls that Neptune built its walls (and now tears them down). The tree-felling image returns elsewhere, for instance in the felling of the forest for Misenus' pyre in 6.179-82.

title: The omen of the flame and the thunder on the left
greek: ecce levis summo de vertice visus Iuli fundere lumen apex ... intonuit laevum
short: A harmless flame plays on Iulus' head; Anchises asks Jupiter to confirm it, and thunder on the left and a shooting star follow. Anchises agrees to leave.
body: A fire on a child's head was a famous Roman omen of future greatness: Livy tells it of Servius Tullius, who became king (Livy 1.39). Apex can mean a cone or tongue of flame, and also the pointed cap of a Roman priest. Anchises follows proper Roman augural procedure: an unsought sign (an oblativum augurium) is confirmed by asking for a second sign. Thunder 'on the left' was favourable in Roman augury (because the Roman augur faced south, the left was the east, the lucky side), whereas Greek practice counted the right as lucky. A shooting star then shows the way to Ida, where the exiles will gather. The omen links the boy Iulus to the destiny of the Julian family and turns Anchises from refusal to consent.

title: Aeneas carries Anchises
greek: ergo age, care pater, cervici imponere nostrae; ipse subibo umeris
short: Aeneas carries his father on his shoulders, leads his son by the hand and has Anchises hold the Penates: the defining image of Roman pietas.
body: The group of Aeneas carrying Anchises, who holds the household gods, while leading Ascanius, was an emblem of pietas known in Italy long before Virgil (it appears on Etruscan vases and statuettes) and was later set up in the Forum of Augustus and shown on coins of Julius Caesar. The three generations in one image show duty to the father, to the gods and to the son. Aeneas will not touch the sacred objects himself until he has washed off blood 'in a living stream' (flumine vivo, running water), a Roman rule of ritual purity after killing. The lion-skin he throws over his shoulders recalls Hercules. Creusa, notably, is told to follow 'afar' (longe), and the arrangement leads directly to her loss.

title: Creusa's ghost and the threefold embrace
greek: ter conatus ibi collo dare bracchia circum; ter frustra comprensa manus effugit imago
short: Creusa, lost in the flight, appears as a ghost larger than life, prophesies Hesperia and a royal bride, and slips three times from Aeneas' arms.
body: Creusa, Priam's daughter and Aeneas' wife, vanishes on the way; Aeneas does not know whether she was 'torn by fate', lost her way or sank down exhausted. Her ghost, 'larger than her wont' (nota maior imago, since the dead appear larger), forbids grief: her fate is willed by Jupiter, and she is spared slavery among the Greeks because 'the mighty mother of the gods' (Cybele, the Phrygian goddess of Mount Ida) keeps her in the Troad. She is the first to name the destination precisely, 'Lydian Tiber' (the Etruscans were believed to have come from Lydia), and a 'king's daughter', Lavinia. The threefold failed embrace translates Odysseus' attempt to embrace his mother's shade (Od. 11.204-8), and Virgil repeats the lines when Aeneas tries to embrace Anchises in the underworld (6.700-2).
